# The Drawer to the Left of the Stove

Every house has one. My mother's was to the left of the stove, and it stuck on humid days, so you had to lift and pull at the same time, a motion I learned before I learned to tie my shoes. The rest of the kitchen has been boxed and labeled. The dishes went to my cousin. The good knives went to my brother, who does not cook but wanted them anyway, which is its own kind of grief. I told everyone I would handle the drawer. I have been handling it for forty minutes, and I have not thrown away a single thing.

**Rubber bands, approximately sixty.** Most came off the morning newspaper, which she took long after everyone else stopped. Some have gone brittle and snap when I touch them. A few are the thick blue ones from broccoli. She saved them the way people who lived through lean years save things: not out of need, but because throwing away something useful felt like a small moral failure. I put them back.

**A birthday candle shaped like the number 7.** Only the 7. I try to work out whose birthday. Mine was 1993. My brother's, 1995. But there's a faint smear of blue frosting on the base, and I remember, suddenly, that it was hers. Her seventieth. She said a 7 and a 0 were too much fuss, so we used just the 7, and my brother said it made her look like a child, and she said, *good.* She blew it out and then licked the frosting off the bottom, which I had forgotten until this exact second.

**Four keys on no ring.** None of them fit anything in this house. I know because I tried, the week after, going door to door like a burglar in reverse. One is small and brass, the kind for a diary or a jewelry box. One says DO NOT DUPLICATE, which feels like instructions I failed to follow. I will never know what they opened. There are rooms in everyone we lose that we were never given keys to, and here they are, the keys, and still no rooms.

**A takeout menu from Golden Dragon**, which closed in 2011. The number for sesame chicken is circled. Beneath it, in her handwriting: *no scallions for D.* I'm D. I've hated scallions since I was six. She wrote it down so she'd never have to remember it, and then remembered it anyway, for thirty years, every time.

**A pen from the Gulf Breeze Motel, Panama City.** We never went to Panama City. Or I never did. I turn it over and over. My parents drove somewhere the year before I was born, a trip she described only as "the one with the flat tire," and I realize now it might have been this. It might have been a honeymoon. It might have been an argument, or an escape, or a week when she was a person I would not have recognized. The pen still works. I write my name on the back of the menu to check.

**Twist ties.** Of course.

**A battery, AA, charge unknown.** This was her great philosophical category. The drawer always had batteries of unknown charge, and when the remote died she would try them one by one, holding each up to the light as if she could see inside. She never labeled the dead ones. She never threw them out. Hope, I think, or stubbornness. In her they were the same muscle.

**A recipe card for lemon bars.** Half of it is in her handwriting, neat and slanting. The second half is in her mother's, older and rounder, in pencil gone silver. They must have written it together, or one started and the other finished, years apart. At the bottom, in my mother's hand, someone added a note: *less sugar than it says, she always made them too sweet.* A small correction across a generation. Tender and a little petty. Exactly like her.

**One earring.** Gold hoop. I know the other is somewhere in this house or in no place at all.

**A matchbook, nearly empty.** Three matches left. I have a strange urge to strike one, and I don't.

**A folded sticky note:** *Call Denise re: Thursday.*

I don't know who Denise is. I don't know which Thursday. It could be from last spring or from a decade ago. What gets me is not the mystery but the confidence of it. *Call Denise.* As if there would always be a call. As if Thursday would always come. And I suppose it did, for her, for a while. Thursday came and she called Denise and they settled whatever needed settling, and the note stayed in the drawer because the drawer was where things went once they no longer mattered but couldn't quite be let go.

That's the thing I understand now, sitting on the kitchen floor with a candle shaped like a 7 in my hand. The drawer was never junk. It was the place for things whose use had passed but whose meaning hadn't. It was a museum with no labels, curated by someone who never intended anyone else to walk through.

My brother will come tomorrow with a truck and ask if I've finished. I'll say almost.

I put everything back. The rubber bands, the keys to nothing, the pen from a motel I will never see. Then I take the Golden Dragon menu, with *no scallions for D* in her writing and my name now scrawled on the back in cheap motel ink, and I fold it into my wallet.

Then I lift and pull, the way she taught me, and close the drawer.

I've settled on "The Drawer to the Left of the Stove," a story told through an inventory of objects found in a mother's junk drawer after her death, letting each item build the narrative through accumulation. I'm listing out the contents—rubber bands, a birthday candle, mystery keys, an old takeout menu, a half-written recipe card, a single earring—and thinking through how the piece should end, then drafting carefully toward the word count.
